total = 0

course.chapter_sub: chapter {n} of Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition
course.chapter_intro: Chapter {n} of Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (Sweigart, 2025), renewed for an advanced course.

playground.label: Guess the number (uses input)

findings: Chapter 3 of the 3rd edition teaches repetition with the while statement, which repeats a block as long as its condition is true, and the for statement with the range() function, which repeats it a counted number of times; break leaves a loop early and continue jumps back to its start. It then shows how to import modules, how sys.exit() ends a program, and two short programs, Guess the Number and Rock, Paper, Scissors.

The reference documentation makes precise what the chapter leaves informal: a for statement evaluates its iterable once and iterates over an iterator made from it; range() returns an immutable arithmetic sequence that generates its values on demand rather than a list; a loop's else clause runs when the loop finishes without a break; the loop variable is overwritten on each pass and is not deleted when the loop ends; and code that modifies a collection while iterating over it is tricky, so the tutorial advises looping over a copy. enumerate() replaces range(len(a)) when both index and item are needed. sys.exit() raises SystemExit, so finally clauses still run. PEP 8 advises against wildcard imports, which agrees with the chapter, and advises imports on separate lines, which the chapter's import random, sys, os, math does not follow. The chapter's practice question on stopping a program stuck in an infinite loop is answered by the KeyboardInterrupt entry: Control-C.

For an advanced course, chapter 3 is best taught as the iteration protocol seen from the loop: a for loop consumes an iterable, range() is one lazy sequence among many, enumerate() and zip() are the idioms that replace index arithmetic, the loop else and the assignment expression are the two features that shorten common loops, and the chapter's while-True-with-break pattern is the one to compare them against.

Python 3.8 added assignment expressions, so a loop can test and name a value in one line - while chunk := file.read(8192): is the PEP's own example of a loop that cannot be trivially rewritten with the two-argument form of iter(). Python 3.10 added an optional strict argument to zip that raises ValueError when the iterables differ in length. Python 3.14 makes the compiler emit a SyntaxWarning when a return, break or continue leaves a finally block.
title: Loops for an advanced course: chapter 3 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Repetition
nodes.body: Chapter 3 is about running a block again: some loops repeat while a condition holds, others once for each item of a sequence (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Condition loop
nodes.body: A condition loop repeats as long as an expression is true, so how many times it runs depends on the program's data rather than on a count (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: While statement
nodes.body: A while statement repeats its block as long as its condition is true; unlike an if statement, execution jumps back to the start of the block, and the yourName.py program keeps asking until the user types the phrase (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A while statement repeats its block as long as its condition is true, and tests the condition again after every pass.

nodes.label: Infinite loop
nodes.body: If the condition never becomes false the program keeps going forever, a common programming bug; written deliberately as while True:, the loop is left by break, return, sys.exit() or an exception (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs until something inside it leaves: break, return, sys.exit() or an exception.

nodes.label: Counted loop
nodes.body: A counted loop runs its block once for each item of a sequence, so its length is known before it starts (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: For statement
nodes.body: A for statement evaluates its iterable once, makes an iterator from it, assigns each item to the target in turn and runs the block, so for i in range(5): runs five times (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A for statement takes each item of an iterable in turn, assigns it to its variable and runs the block once for each.

nodes.label: Sequence
nodes.body: Loops need something to iterate over, and range() is the chapter's way of making a sequence of integers (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Range sequence
nodes.body: The range function makes an arithmetic progression of integers and takes one, two or three arguments (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Range stop
nodes.body: With one argument range starts at 0 and stops before the argument, so list(range(5)) is [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] and the end point is never part of the sequence (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: range(n) yields the integers from 0 up to but not including n.

nodes.label: Range start stop
nodes.body: With two arguments range begins at the first and stops before the second, so list(range(12, 16)) is [12, 13, 14, 15]; range(10), range(0, 10) and range(0, 10, 1) all give the same values (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: range(start, stop) begins at start and ends before stop.

nodes.label: Range step
nodes.body: A third argument sets the step, so list(range(0, 10, 2)) is [0, 2, 4, 6, 8] (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A third argument is the step between values.

nodes.label: Range descending
nodes.body: A negative step counts down, and the stop value is still excluded, so list(range(5, -1, -1)) is [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0] (Sweigart, 2025).
nodes.definition: A negative step counts down, and the stop value is still excluded.

nodes.label: Lazy range
nodes.body: Printing a range shows range(0, 10), not the numbers: it behaves like a list in many ways but is an object that returns successive items when iterated, which saves space (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: A range is an object that produces its values when iterated, not a list holding them.

nodes.label: Iteration helper
nodes.body: Two built-in functions replace most index arithmetic in loops: one adds a count, the other walks several sequences together (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Enumerate function
nodes.body: When a loop needs both the position and the item, enumerate gives them as pairs, so list(enumerate(['tic', 'tac', 'toe'])) is [(0, 'tic'), (1, 'tac'), (2, 'toe')]; the tutorial prefers it to combining range and len (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: enumerate pairs each item with a running count, replacing range(len(a)) when both are needed.

nodes.label: Zip strict
nodes.body: zip walks several iterables together and by default stops at the shortest; since Python 3.10 zip(..., strict=True) raises ValueError when the lengths differ, which turns a silent truncation into an error (Bucher, 2020).
nodes.definition: zip walks several iterables together; strict=True raises ValueError when their lengths differ instead of stopping at the shortest.

nodes.label: Loop control
nodes.body: Three statements and one function change how a loop runs or ends: break, continue, the loop's else clause and sys.exit() (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Early exit
nodes.body: Some programs must leave a loop, or the whole program, before the loop's own test would (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Break statement
nodes.body: The break statement ends the innermost enclosing for or while loop at once, and skips the loop's else clause; yourName2.py uses it to leave a while True: loop (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: break ends the innermost enclosing loop at once and skips the loop's else clause.

nodes.label: Exit function
nodes.body: sys.exit() raises SystemExit, so it ends the program only when nothing intercepts the exception and only from the main thread; finally clauses still run, and an argument of None or 0 means success while a string is printed to standard error with exit status 1 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: sys.exit() raises SystemExit, which ends the program unless something intercepts it; finally clauses still run.

nodes.label: Skipping
nodes.body: Skipping a pass is different from leaving the loop: the loop continues (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Continue statement
nodes.body: The continue statement skips the rest of the block and goes back to test the condition of a while loop, or to take the next item of a for loop; swordfish.py uses it to keep asking for a name (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: continue skips the rest of the block and goes back to test the condition, or to take the next item.

nodes.label: Loop completion
nodes.body: How a loop finishes can be told apart from how it was left, and what the loop variable holds afterwards is defined (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Loop else clause
nodes.body: The else clause of a for or while loop runs when the loop finishes without executing break, and is skipped by a break, a return or a raised exception; it is the tidy way to say 'searched everything and found nothing' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: An else clause on a loop runs when the loop finishes without executing break.

nodes.label: Loop variable scope
nodes.body: The for statement overwrites its target on every pass, so assigning to it inside the block does not change the loop, and the name is not deleted when the loop ends; after a loop over an empty sequence it was never assigned (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: The loop variable is overwritten on each pass and is not deleted when the loop ends; after a loop over an empty sequence it was never assigned.

nodes.label: Module
nodes.body: A program reaches the standard library's functions by importing the module that holds them (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Import form
nodes.body: The chapter shows three forms of the import statement, and PEP 8 has a view on each (Sweigart, 2025) (Van Rossum et al., 2001).

nodes.label: Import statement
nodes.body: The import statement makes a module's names available under the module's name, so after import random a program calls random.randint(1, 10), which returns an integer N with 1 <= N <= 10 (Sweigart, 2025) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.definition: import makes a module's names available under the module's name, as random.randint(1, 10).

nodes.label: Multiple import
nodes.body: The chapter lets one statement import several modules, as in import random, sys, os, math (Sweigart, 2025); PEP 8 says imports should usually be on separate lines (Van Rossum et al., 2001).
nodes.definition: One import statement can name several modules separated by commas.

nodes.label: Star import
nodes.body: from random import * removes the module prefix, but the chapter itself concludes that using the full name makes for more readable code (Sweigart, 2025), and PEP 8 says wildcard imports should be avoided because they make it unclear which names are present (Van Rossum et al., 2001).
nodes.definition: from module import * brings every public name into the program without the module prefix.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: An advanced course pairs the chapter's loops with what current Python offers for the same jobs, and with the hazards the reference documentation names (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Expression style
nodes.body: Two recent language and style features shorten and tidy the loops and imports the chapter teaches (Angelico et al., 2018).

nodes.label: Assignment expression loop
nodes.body: Since Python 3.8 an assignment expression names a value inside a condition, so while chunk := file.read(8192): process(chunk) reads and tests in one line - the PEP's own example of a loop that cannot be trivially rewritten with a two-argument iter() (Angelico et al., 2018).
nodes.definition: An assignment expression names a value inside a condition, so a loop can read and test in one line.

nodes.label: Import style
nodes.body: PEP 8 advises one import per line and says wildcard imports should be avoided, with the single defensible exception of republishing an internal interface as part of a public API (Van Rossum et al., 2001).
nodes.example: import os on one line, import sys on the next
nodes.definition: PEP 8 advises one import per line and against wildcard imports.

nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.body: Two hazards the documentation names are worth teaching beside the chapter's programs (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Mutation while iterating
nodes.body: Code that modifies a collection while iterating over that same collection can be tricky to get right; the tutorial's remedy is to loop over a copy, such as users.copy().items(), or to build a new collection (Python Software Foundation, 2026).
nodes.example: for user in users: del users[user]
nodes.definition: Changing a collection while iterating over it is tricky to get right; loop over a copy or build a new collection.

nodes.label: Finally exit
nodes.body: Python 3.14 makes the compiler emit a SyntaxWarning when a return, break or continue statement has the effect of leaving a finally block, as PEP 765 specifies (Katriel and Coghlan, 2024).
nodes.definition: Python 3.14 emits a SyntaxWarning when return, break or continue leaves a finally block.
